zaara.c: ZAARA, one of the divisions of Africa, situated under the tropic of cancer, is bounded by Bildulgerid on the north, by the unknown parts of Africa on thee aft, by Nigritia or Negrolaad on the south, and by the Atlantic ocean on the weft. This is a barren desert, and so destitute of water, that the e-amels which pass over it from Morocco to traffic with Negroland, are half loaded with water and provifioos.

zaffer.c:
ZAFFER, or Zafre, in chemistry, the name of a blue substance, of the hardness and form of a stone ; and generally suppo fed to be a native fossil.

It is in reality, however, a preparation of cobalt ; the calx of that mineral being mixed with powdered flints and wetted with wa^er to bring it into this form.

ZEAL, the exercise of a warm animated affection, or passion, for any thing.

ZEALAND the chief of the Danish islands, is situated at the entrance of t e Baltic-sea, hounded by the Schaggerrac-sea on the north ; by the Sound, which separates it from Schonen, on the east ; by the Baltic-sea, on the south ; and by the strait called the Great Belt, which separates it from the "island of Funen, on the weft; being of a round figure, near two hundred miles in circum se rence : the chief town is Copenhagen.

Zealand, is also a province of the United Netherlands, confiding of e>ght islands, which lie in the mouth of the river Scheld, bounded by the province of Holland, from which they are separated by a narrow channel, on the north ; by Brabant, on the east ; by Flanders, from which they are separated by one of the branches of the Scheld, on the south ; and by the German ocean, on the •wed.

ZEALOTS, an ancient se<5t of the Jews, so called from their pretended zeal for God’s law, and the honour of religion.

zechariah.c: ZECHARIAH, a canonical book of the Old Testament, containing the predictions of Zechariah, the fon of Barachia, and grandson of Iddo. He is the eleventh of the twelve se lier prophets. Zecharuh entered upon the prophetic office at the same time withTLggai, and was sent to the Jews upon the same me stage, to reprove them for their backwardness in erecting the temple, and restoring divine worst lip ; but. especially for the disorder of their lives and manners, which could not but derive a curie upon them. By feveral notable visions and types, he endeavours to confirm their faith, and establish their affuran e concerning God’s providence with them, and c are over them ; and as a proof and demonftr'aticn of this, he intersperses the mod comfortable promises o* the cojr.ingof the kingdom, the temple, the priiftho d the victory, the glory of Ch lift' the Branch. Nor does he forget to allure them of the ruin of Babylon, their most inv pia cable enemy. This prophet is the longest and rood obscure of all the lefLr prophets, his style being interrupted and without connexion.

zedoary.c:
ZEDOARY, in the materia medica, a root, the feveral pieces of which differ so much from one another in shape, that they have been divided into two kinds, as if two different things, under the names of the long and round zedoary, being ony the feveral parts of the lame root.

Zedoary is to be chosen fresh: found, and hard, in Urge pieces ; it matters not as to shape, whether long or round ; of a fmooih surface, and of a sort of fat ty appearance whin, too hard to be bitten by the teeth, and of the brisk eft smell that may be ; such as is friable, dusty, and worm eaten, is to be rejected.

Zedoary, both of the long and round kind, Is brought us from China; and we find by the Arabians, that they also had it from the same place. The round tubera are lefs frequent than the long, and some of them have therefore supposed them the produce of a different and more rare plant ;’but this is not so probable as that the general form of the root ts long, ar.d the round tubera are only lufus naturae, and lefs frequent in it.

Zedoary, distilled with common water, affords a thick and dense* est entail oil, which soon concretes of itself into a kind ot camphor, and on this oil its virtues principally depend. It is a sudorific, and is much recommended by some in fevers, especially of the malignant kinds. It is also given with success as an expectorant in all disorders of the breast, arising from a tough phlegm, which it powerfully incides and attenuates ; it is also good against flatulences, and in the cholic ; it ftxengthens the stomach, and assists digestion ; and, finally, is given Avith success in nervous cafes of all kinds.

zend.c:
ZEND, or Zendavesta, a book containing the religioa of the Magians, or worshippers of fire* who were disciples of the famous Zoroaster. See Magi.

This book was composed by Zoroaftcrduring his retirement in a cave, and contained all the pretended revelations of that impostor. The first part contains the liturgy of the ma$, which is used among them in all their, oratories and fire-temples to this day; they reverence it as the Christians do the Bible, and the Mahometans the Koran. There are found many things in the zend taken out of the scriptures. of the Old Testament, which Df. PVidcaux thinks is an argument that Zoroaster was originally a Jew. Great part of the Psalms of David are inferred: he makes Adam and Eve to have been the firlb parents of mankind, and gives the same history of the creation and deluge as Mosies does, and commands the same observances about clean and unclean beads, the same law of paying tythes to the sacerdotal order, with many other inftiiutions of Jewish extraction. The reft of its contents are an historical account of the life, a&sons, and proph cies of its author, with rules and exhortations to moral living The Mahometans have a fed which they call Zendikites, who are said to be the Sadducees of Mahometanism, denying providence and the resurrection, beZ O D ( 953 ) Z y G

Jieving the transmigration of souls, and following the zend of the magi, ,

ZEPHANIAH, a canonical book of the Old Tedament,

‘ containing the predictions of Zephaniah the fon of Cushi, and grandson of Gedaliah ; being the ninth of the twelve lesser prophets. He prop heeded in the time of king Josiah, a little after the captivity of the ten tribes, and before that of Judah; so that he was co-temporary with Jeremiah. He freely publhhes to the Jews, that what increased the divine wrath against them, was their contempt of God’s service, their apodacy, their treachery, their idolatry, their violence and rapine, and other enor* rrities: such hi^h provocations as these rendered their deftrudlion terrible, universal, and unavoidable : and then, as most of the prophets do, he ming les exhortations with repentance, as the only expedient in these circumdances.
